- If sentiment is negative (≤ -0.5) in recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is positive (≥ 0.5) and price is trending down, model often underestimates the drop; adjust downward bias by 5–10% of recent mean.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 2–5% per day post-spike.
- When true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 60), model often ignores it; add a “reversion buffer” to forecast: if 3 days below 60, cap forecast at 60–62.
- If sentiment is neutral (0.0) and forecast is rising steadily, model often fails to account for volatility; add a 1–2% downward volatility buffer to avoid overconfidence.
- For 30-day horizon, model tends to overestimate early in the period (first 5–7 days) when sentiment is flat; apply a “lag correction”: subtract 1–2% from first 5 days if sentiment is neutral or weak.
